_work.title: Shams al-Ma'arif — The Sun of Knowledge (Ahmad al-Buni)
_work.blurb: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni's (d. 622/1225) Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra (The Great Sun of Knowledge) is the most influential Arabic grimoire and the foundational text of Islamicate lettrism (huruf). It systematizes the occult properties of the 28 Arabic letters, the 99 Names of God, magic squares (awfaq), and planetary talismans into a vast cosmological system. Buni synthesizes Sufi cosmology, astrological magic, and Neoplatonic letter-mysticism into a practical manual for divine invocation and natural magic. The text circulated in hundreds of manuscript copies across the Islamic world from Morocco to Central Asia, and was central to the practices of Sufi orders, court magicians, and popular healers alike.

entries.title: Shams al-Ma'arif — Manuscript Opening, Early 17th Century
entries.rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 / GFDL. Photograph by Danieliness, cropped by User:User-duck.
entries.summary: An opening page of a manuscript copy of Ahmad al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra (The Great Sun of Knowledge), dating to the early 17th century. Al-Buni (d. 622/1225 CE) compiled this encyclopedic Arabic grimoire in North Africa or Egypt, synthesizing Islamic Sufi cosmology, astrological magic, letter mysticism (huruf), and the practical use of magic squares (awfaq) and divine names. The manuscript shows the characteristic dense Arabic calligraphy, chapter headings in bold naskh or thuluth script, and geometric interlace decorations that mark luxury copies of the Shams al-Ma'arif. The text was the most widely copied Arabic magical handbook in history, existing in hundreds of MSS across the Islamic world.
